🐾 Here’s Matt’s payments work—from the payment engine to the developer experience.

His work spans Execution & Delivery and Org & Working-Model Transformation, with engagements at **JP Morgan Chase** and **American Express**.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, corporate treasurers were working across separate regional systems. ACCESS Next Generation used Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform, but the bank needed payment capabilities beyond its out-of-box offering for **135,000+** clients across **180+** countries. Each payment type had different formatting, validation, compliance, and workflow requirements.

Matt led a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and the bank, with engineers in Mumbai, Bangalore, and the US. He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and tax payment modules, alongside payment verification, granular permissions, sanctions screening, and contextual help. That inline guidance explained wire fields, tax codes, and cross-border requirements to reduce errors and support calls.

He also designed the centralized gateway connecting payment channels across **12** countries. Corporate treasurers gained a single entry point for payments across regions, rather than separate local logins. Matt led the payments data migration, preserving client configurations, entitlements, transaction histories, and compliance traceability **without disruption to live payment operations**. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**.

At **American Express**, the Virtual Payments Platform was replacing a legacy mainframe, but clients—particularly those without mature development teams—faced missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, and no sandbox. Developers also faced dependency bottlenecks and delayed testing.

Matt co-created a developer portal with Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, sample integrations, use case-driven documentation, and a secure sandbox. He introduced environment virtualization for earlier testing, used Lean Product and XP practices, and conducted a Client Onboarding Test Drive to gather user feedback.

API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch. Onboarding time and integration complexity decreased, testing became more reliable, and the portal team delivered over **261** additional story points of customer-focused value.

Matt ran UAT and production validation/shakeout testing and triaged those defects. Across releases, waves, and migrations, he owned **Sev-1** incident response, coordinating root-cause analysis with the bank, offshore engineers, and Bottomline’s vendor team while running status updates and daily leadership calls. The stories do not specify outage duration, affected transaction counts, or financial losses. The migration itself was completed without disruption to live payment operations.

At **American Express**, the problem was that clients struggled to evaluate and integrate the Virtual Payments Platform: SDKs were missing, documentation was fragmented, and there was no sandbox. Dependency bottlenecks and delayed testing also slowed API integration and onboarding.

Matt co-created SDKs, use case-driven documentation, and a secure sandbox, and introduced environment virtualization for earlier testing. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch. Onboarding time decreased, testing reliability improved, and the portal team exceeded its delivery commitment by over **261 story points**.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt describes—and practices—his leadership.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose, with a “permit to fail” learning environment and balanced teams: Product + Engineering + Design together. His work spans Execution & Delivery, Org & Working-Model Transformation, and Talent & Enablement.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, teams faced knowledge gaps as cloud-native technologies evolved. Matt paired senior engineers with junior team members, established weekly tech talks with peer-led demos, and embedded learning within live client projects. He created tailored skill development plans and career progression frameworks. Retention improved and new hires onboarded faster; those results weren’t quantified in the story. He built the Atlanta and Tampa centers from zero to **150+ practitioners**, with recruiting, training, budget management, and full P&L accountability.

With enterprise clients, he addressed “same silos, same handoffs, same bottlenecks” rather than treating modernization as just a technology change. He coached teams using “I do, we do, you do” and ran **6-week** Agility Coaching Labs on their actual work. Clients adopted self-regulating balanced teams and reduced costs **15–35%**. He also brought product owners and team leads into prioritization workshops, with measurable objectives, regular backlog refinement, and visible progress dashboards.

At **Capital One**, internal teams were overwhelmed and experiencing burnout under regulatory deadlines. Matt assembled a balanced team of **8**, organized Go upskilling, and embedded pair programming, continuous integration, and automated testing. His teams delivered defect-free production code at **4x** the output of internal teams. Across financial-services engagements, he made security tradeoffs visible and embedded security requirements into the Definition of Done; teams achieved **100% compliance** with PCI DSS, GDPR, and SOX.

Matt also acknowledges that he previously led at an unsustainable pace. After leaving **Accenture**, he defined clearer boundaries and prioritized health, recovery, and focus. His stated commitment now is to build teams where “sustainable pace is expected, not exceptional.”

answer_md:
🐾 At **Norfolk Southern**, the balanced-team setup and emphasis on test-driven development did not prevent a quality crisis.

Early in **2020**, Matt launched the Cloud Innovation Center’s first major engagement to modernize the client’s Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A couple of months in, as the pandemic shifted work to remote, the client reported rising defects—even though dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The credibility hit landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership.

An engineer had been building from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. Coverage looked complete, but defects went undetected. The backlog also contained vague stories without defined scenarios or a definition of done. Matt’s initial emphasis on TDD had not established the actual test-first practice.

Matt took ownership in front of the client and account leadership. Instead of defending the dashboard, he ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and showed the gaps openly—including the backlog problems. He rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work side by side with the team, redoing code and tests. Boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and “I do, we do, you do” pairing followed.

Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. The story does not quantify that reduction. Client confidence was restored through the open audit and visible improvement—not through the initial process setup alone.

answer_md:
🐾 Yes—at **Norfolk Southern**, the balanced-team and test-driven development approach initially fell short.

In early **2020**, Matt launched the Cloud Innovation Center’s first major engagement: modernizing the Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A couple of months in, as the pandemic forced remote work, the client reported rising defects. The dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The problem reached both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

Matt had emphasized test-driven development, but the team wasn’t consistently practicing it. An engineer was solutioning from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story and writing tests after the code. Coverage looked complete while defects went undetected. The backlog also contained vague stories without defined scenarios or a definition of done.

Matt took ownership in front of the client and account leadership. Rather than defending the coverage metrics, he ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and showed the gaps openly—including the backlog problems. He rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work side by side with the team, redoing code and test cases.

He also introduced Samman-style coaching: boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and pairing through “I do, we do, you do.”

Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Matt’s stated lesson was that “metrics mean nothing without the practice behind them,” and that cultural transformation requires consistent coaching, not just process change.

🐾 Yes—team autonomy at the Cloud Innovation Center didn’t work consistently as it scaled.

At **Accenture**, Matt designed the center to be flat from day one: autonomy at the team level, collective ownership, and minimal middle layers. But designing the model was not the same as living it. Many practitioners came from legacy delivery organizations where top-down, command-and-control patterns were the norm. Those habits reasserted themselves: decisions drifted upward, teams waited for direction, and bottlenecks formed where autonomy was supposed to be. Converting people to the model took enforcement and revalidation, multiple times; the path was bumpy.

The “permit to fail” culture also wasn’t universal. As the centers scaled to **150+ practitioners**, isolated pockets of fear of blame emerged. Some team members still hesitated to share ideas or take risks, limiting innovation and engagement in those areas.

Matt responded by giving cross-functional teams explicit decision-making authority and creating clear, flexible guidelines tied to project objectives. Anchors and team leads focused on removing obstacles rather than controlling outcomes. He used continuous retrospectives to revisit how teams were working, engaged directly with team members about their challenges, and shared his own experiences with risk-taking and mistakes rather than only asking others to be open.

The stories report fewer decision bottlenecks, higher engagement, improved morale, and reduced turnover after those changes. They do not give numerical measures for those improvements or describe a specific failed client delivery. The documented problem was that the intended working model repeatedly slipped back into centralized decisions and fear of blame—not that autonomy was established once and stayed in place.

🐾 Here's the payments work.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, Matt worked on ACCESS Next Generation, replacing separate regional treasury and cash-management systems with a unified corporate banking portal. The bank served **135,000+** corporations, financial institutions, governments, and municipalities across **180+** countries. Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform was the foundation, but payment formatting, validation, compliance, and workflow requirements went well beyond its out-of-box capabilities.

Matt managed a blended team of **40+** **Accenture** and bank resources across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore, working extensively from Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices. He designed and delivered ACH credits and direct debits, wire payments, FX/cross-border payments, and federal tax payments. He implemented Message Authentication Code payment verification, payment-type-specific entitlements, sanctions screening, and risk-based approval controls. His work also covered real-time global reporting, single sign-on across treasury functions, and trade finance integration.

For the global payments gateway, he designed message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across payment networks in **12 countries**, connecting ACCESS to internal compliance, settlement, and reporting systems. He also led payments data migration, preserving client configurations, entitlement structures, transaction histories, and compliance traceability. The migration completed **without disruption to live payment operations**. ACCESS and its Integrated Global Payments Interface launched in **April 2011**; Matt also owned on-call incident response and production validation during rollout.

At **American Express**, his work focused on adoption of the Virtual Payments Platform replacing a legacy mainframe system. Clients faced missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, no sandbox, and delayed testing. Matt co-created a developer portal, developed Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, and built a secure sandbox with refreshed client data. He introduced environment virtualization, use-case-driven documentation, Lean Product and XP practices, and a Client Onboarding Test Drive.

API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, and client onboarding time decreased. The portal modernization team exceeded its delivery commitment by **over 261 story points** of customer-focused value.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt describes—and practices—his leadership.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. His own wording is “listen first, align around purpose, and move intentionally.” He describes a “permit to fail” learning environment and balanced teams: Product + Engineering + Design together. His leadership work includes Org & Working-Model Transformation and Talent & Enablement, alongside Execution & Delivery.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Centers, building an organization meant more than directing delivery. The organization grew from a **10-person** pilot to **150+ practitioners**, but managers deliberately did not sit on daily teams. Matt kept the structure flat through **11–13** direct-report practice and client leads. Teams held execution power, with collective code ownership, fluid role rotation, and experienced engineering anchors keeping leads informed without adding a middle-management layer.

Instead of evaluating people through a manager’s impressions, Matt built a peer-driven feedback system. Recent pair partners, product managers, and anchors supplied evidence about communication, knowledge sharing, and how people integrated feedback. He personally ran monthly feedback capture sessions. Advancement depended on contributions to daily teammates, not visibility to a boss.

He paired senior engineers with junior team members, embedded learning in live client projects, and established weekly peer-led demos and engineering practice forums. Friday afternoons were reserved for practice leads’ career-development conversations. Matt also made every final hiring decision, allocated compensation, facilitated promotion calibration, and owned decisions to end performance remediation.

The organization recorded near-zero attrition in its first **2 years**. During scaling pushes, hiring sustained **4–6 net-new practitioners per week**, with interview participation capped at **2 slots per practitioner per week** to protect delivery and avoid burnout.

🐾 Here’s Matt’s payments work at **JP Morgan Chase** and **American Express**.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, ACCESS Next Generation needed more than an out-of-box deployment of Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform. Corporate treasurers needed different formatting, validation, compliance, and approval workflows for each payment type. Regional systems also had different data models and connectivity to payment networks.

Matt led a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and **JP Morgan Chase**, working directly with Bottomline in Portsmouth. He managed the build-versus-configure boundary: determining where WebSeries’ native capabilities ended and bespoke engineering was required. He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules, including NACHA file validation, Message Authentication Code security, and payment-type-specific entitlements. A user could be authorized for wire approval but not FX initiation. He also integrated sanctions screening and customer risk scores into payment controls.

For the gateway, Matt designed message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**, connecting payment rails with internal compliance, settlement, and reporting systems. He also led payments data migration, preserving client configurations, entitlement structures, transaction histories, and regulatory traceability. The migration completed without disruption to live payment operations. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,000+** clients across **180+ countries**.

At **American Express**, the Virtual Payments Platform was replacing a legacy mainframe, but adoption lagged: clients lacked SDKs, documentation was fragmented, and there was no sandbox. Dependency bottlenecks also delayed testing.

Matt co-created a developer portal with Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, sample integrations, use case-driven documentation, and a secure sandbox. He introduced environment virtualization so developers could test earlier without waiting on downstream systems. Discovery and Framing workshops, Lean Product and XP practices, and a Client Onboarding Test Drive guided the portal redesign.

API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, and client onboarding time decreased. The portal modernization team also delivered over **261 additional story points** beyond its delivery commitment.

🐾 Here’s how Matt describes—and puts into practice—his leadership style.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. His work spans Execution & Delivery, Org & Working-Model Transformation, and Talent & Enablement. He describes inherited engineering teams as “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” He works to remove those barriers: make intent explicit, build psychological safety so people speak honestly, and push decisions to the people closest to the work.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Centers, Matt ran a deliberately flat organization of **150+** practitioners through **11–13** practice and client leads. Balanced teams brought Product, Engineering, and Design together, with team-level autonomy, collective code ownership, and pair rotation rather than additional management layers. Teams accelerated delivery **4x** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices.

He also changed how performance was evaluated. Because managers did not sit on daily teams, feedback came from recent pair partners, product managers, and team anchors—not just a supervisor’s impressions. Matt ran monthly feedback capture sessions and made expectations explicit by career level. Advancement rested on peer evidence rather than visibility to a boss. The organization recorded near-zero attrition in its first **2 years**.

For development, he paired senior engineers with junior teammates, established peer-led tech talks, and embedded learning in live client projects. With client teams, he used “I do, we do, you do” coaching and **6-week** Agility Coaching Labs on their actual work. Restructuring client teams around business domains reduced costs **15–35%**.

Autonomy did not remove accountability. Matt owned final hiring decisions, compensation allocation, and end-of-remediation calls. He also owned engagement economics: at **Fiserv**, he helped recover an **\$8.5M** program to **3% under budget**, avoiding **\$500K** in penalties. At **JP Morgan Chase**, he established migration planning and program controls for **341** applications. He also created hands-on enablement content that trained **300+** professionals.

He de-emphasized individual accolades and recognized contributions that advanced shared project goals.

Decentralized decision-making removed bottlenecks, allowing teams to act faster. Teams reported higher engagement and satisfaction, with improved retention and project stability. The brainstorming sessions also produced more efficient ways to reach project milestones and improvements to timelines and quality.

🐾 Here's Matt's payments work at **JP Morgan Chase** and **American Express**.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, ACCESS Next Generation needed more than Bottomline Technologies’ out-of-box WebSeries platform. Regional payment systems had different formats, protocols, entitlement structures, and compliance records. The new portal had to serve **135,000+** clients across **180+** countries while live payment processing continued.

Matt was Technology Delivery Lead, managing a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and the bank. He designed and delivered bespoke ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and government tax payment modules. That included NACHA file validation, embedded FX rate visibility, Message Authentication Code security, and payment-type-specific permissions—for example, allowing wire approval without allowing FX initiation. He also integrated sanctions screening and customer risk scores into payment flows and approval requirements.

Rather than retain fragmented regional connections, Matt designed a centralized gateway for message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12** countries. He led the payments data migration, preserving client configurations, transaction histories, and compliance traceability with **zero disruption** to live payment operations. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, giving corporate treasurers a single portal for payments, global reporting, and treasury functions.

At **American Express**, the Virtual Payments Platform was replacing a legacy mainframe system, but adoption lagged: clients faced missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, no sandbox, and delayed testing caused by downstream dependencies.

Matt co-created a developer portal with Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, sample integrations, use case-driven documentation, and a secure sandbox with refreshed client data. He introduced environment virtualization so developers could test earlier, used Lean Product and XP practices, and conducted a Client Onboarding Test Drive to gather user feedback. CI/CD kept documentation and APIs synchronized with backend changes.

API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, onboarding time decreased, and the portal modernization team delivered over **261 additional story points** beyond its commitment.

His work spans Execution & Delivery and Emerging Tech: building payment engines and gateways, consolidating legacy systems, and changing how developers integrate with virtual payments.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, ACCESS Next Generation needed more than Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform provided out of the box. Different payment types had distinct formatting, validation, compliance, and workflow requirements. Regional systems also had different data models and connectivity to payment networks.

Matt managed a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and **JP Morgan Chase**, working across Mumbai, Bangalore, and the US. He designed and delivered bespoke ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and tax-payment modules. He added Message Authentication Code security, payment-type-specific permissions, sanctions screening, and risk-based approval controls. Corporate treasurers could initiate cross-currency payments with embedded rate visibility rather than move between separate treasury platforms.

He also designed the centralized payments gateway: message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**. For the legacy migration, he oversaw consolidation of client configurations, entitlements, and transaction histories, introduced compliance dashboards, and owned production validation and defect triage. The migration completed without disruption to live payment operations. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,000+** clients across **180+ countries**.

At **American Express**, the Virtual Payments Platform was replacing a legacy mainframe system, but adoption lagged: SDKs were missing, documentation was fragmented, and clients had no sandbox. Matt co-created a developer portal, developed Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, and built a secure sandbox with refreshed client data. CI/CD kept documentation and APIs updated alongside backend changes.

The portal modernization also used environment virtualization to reduce downstream dependencies and enable earlier testing, Lean Product and XP practices, and a Client Onboarding Test Drive. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch; onboarding time decreased. The modernization team delivered over **261 additional story points** beyond its delivery commitment.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s an example from **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center.

The center was designed flat from day one: autonomy at the team level, collective ownership, and minimal middle layers. But designing the model was not the same as living it. Many practitioners came from legacy delivery organizations where top-down, command-and-control patterns were the norm. Those habits reasserted themselves: decisions drifted upward, teams waited for direction, and bottlenecks formed where autonomy was supposed to be. Converting people to the model took enforcement and revalidation, multiple times, and the path was bumpy.

Matt established cross-functional teams of product managers, designers, and engineers with shared ownership and decision-making authority. Rather than making leaders the decision-makers, he had them act as facilitators. Anchors and team leads focused on removing obstacles rather than controlling outcomes. He created clear, flexible guidelines so teams could make decisions within project objectives, then used continuous retrospectives and user feedback to help them adjust their work.

As the centers scaled to **150+ practitioners**, pockets of fear of blame also emerged. Matt held open retrospectives focused on growth-oriented feedback and shared his own experiences with risk-taking and mistakes. Team members could voice concerns and challenge assumptions without fear of judgment.

Decentralized decision-making removed bottlenecks. Teams reported higher engagement and satisfaction, and the work on psychological safety improved morale and reduced turnover.

🐾 Here’s an example from **JP Morgan Chase**’s Identity & Access Management Uplift.

Following the **2014** data breach, **341** corporate and investment banking applications needed new security controls. Application teams had to absorb the remediation alongside existing delivery commitments, with no additional staffing or budget planned. Many teams had no prior exposure to role-based access control or access certification; they needed education before they could act.

Matt reached out to application owners and business owners to explain the uplift objectives and what each team needed to do. He taught the security fundamentals, then led application-by-application analysis to establish the current state, assess the impact of the requirements, and define a remediation path.

Rather than give every application the same treatment, he tailored those paths to its technology stack, sunset dates, risk profile, and feasibility. He worked with line-of-business RBAC leads and compliance stakeholders to keep the plans consistent with regulatory requirements. When application teams couldn’t absorb the implementation work alone, he coordinated developer “tiger teams” to augment them without derailing their existing commitments.

The **341**-application portfolio moved from zero awareness of the requirements to active remediation planning and execution. The engagement was cut short by funding constraints, so Matt’s work included a structured handoff of in-progress work and remediation plans to the bank’s internal teams—not a claim that every application’s remediation was completed.

🐾 Here’s Matt’s payments work—from the payment engine to developer onboarding.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, ACCESS Next Generation needed more than an out-of-box deployment of Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform. Regional payment systems had different data models, message formats, entitlement structures, and compliance requirements. The corporate banking portal had to serve **135,000+** corporations, financial institutions, governments, and municipalities across **180+ countries** while keeping live payment operations running.

Matt managed a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and bank resources in the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He designed and delivered bespoke ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and tax payment modules, including NACHA file validation, payment-type-specific permissions, and Message Authentication Code security controls. He also built sanctions screening and incorporated customer risk scores into payment entitlements and approval routing.

Alongside the payment engine, Matt designed the centralized gateway for message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**. He led the payments data migration, preserving client configurations, transaction histories, and compliance traceability. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**; the gateway replaced fragmented regional integrations, and the migration completed **without disruption to live payment operations**. Matt also owned on-call and critical production incident response.

At **American Express**, the Virtual Payments Platform was replacing a legacy mainframe, but adoption lagged: clients lacked SDKs, documentation was fragmented, and there was no sandbox. Dependency bottlenecks also delayed integration testing.

Matt co-created the developer portal, developed Java, .NET, and Python SDKs with sample integrations and “day-one” guides, and built a secure sandbox with refreshed client data. He introduced virtualized testing environments, used Lean Product and XP practices, and conducted a Client Onboarding Test Drive to gather feedback.

API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, onboarding time decreased, and the portal team delivered **over 261 additional story points** beyond its delivery commitment. The stories do not quantify the onboarding reduction.

🐾 Here’s how Matt describes—and puts into practice—his leadership style.

Matt leads with “empathy, clarity, and modern engineering rigor.” His leadership work spans Org & Working-Model Transformation, Talent & Enablement, and Execution & Delivery. He describes inheriting teams that were “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” He makes intent explicit, builds psychological safety so people can speak honestly, and pushes decisions to the people closest to the work.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Centers, he ran a deliberately flat organization of **150+** practitioners through **11–13** practice and client leads. Balanced teams of product, engineering, and design held execution power. Collective code ownership and rotating pairs distributed knowledge across teams rather than through managers. Teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices.

Because managers did not sit beside practitioners daily, Matt built evaluations around evidence from recent pair partners, product managers, and team anchors—not visibility to the boss. He ran monthly feedback sessions, made expectations explicit by career level, and held the final hiring decision on every offer. Performance gaps received direct feedback, coaching, and, when necessary, formal plans with measurable milestones. The organization recorded **near-zero attrition in its first 2 years**.

His coaching used “I do, we do, you do.” He paired senior engineers with junior colleagues, embedded learning in live client projects, and established weekly peer-led demos. With client teams, he ran **6-week** Agility Coaching Labs on their actual work rather than changing technology while leaving the same silos and handoffs intact. Those operating-model engagements reduced costs **15–35%**.

He also owned financial decisions: at the centers, he rejected a request for **2** external contractors and required cross-skilling and redeployment of **2** internal bench resources instead. The decision was escalated, and it stood.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s an example from the Cloud Innovation Center.

Matt describes himself as a “builder.” At **Accenture**, his work included helping clients change how their teams operated—not just replacing their technology. Clients were modernizing systems while keeping the same silos, handoffs, and bottlenecks. They were recreating legacy dysfunction in new systems and wondering why transformation still felt so hard.

Matt worked with technology executives to shift from IT-centric to product-centric operating models. He delivered Product-Centric Operating Model Playbook workshops to assess organizational maturity and address governance, team organization, methodology, and funding. He helped leadership see the difference between “we want agile” and how their teams were actually organized, including how team structure was shaping their architecture.

Instead of relying on workshops alone, he ran **6-week** Agility Coaching Labs with client teams on their actual work. He coached teams using “I do, we do, you do,” pairing with them as they adopted a product mindset and new ways of working. He established success criteria beyond delivery milestones: minimize time to value, solve for need, excel at change, and understand that the product is never done.

Across these operating-model engagements, restructuring into lean, self-regulating balanced teams aligned to business domains reduced costs **15–35%**. Clients continued using balanced teams, OKRs, and lean product practices after the engagements ended.

He also worked with line-of-business RBAC leads and compliance stakeholders on the SOX/SSAE16 requirements.

When funding constraints cut the **Accenture** engagement short, Matt’s team provided a structured handoff of in-progress work and remediation plans to **JP Morgan Chase’s** internal teams—not a claim that the entire remediation was completed.

🐾 Here’s Matt’s payments work across corporate banking, card processing, and virtual payments.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, ACCESS Next Generation needed payment capabilities beyond Bottomline’s WebSeries platform. Different payment types had distinct formatting, validation, compliance, and workflow requirements; connectivity across **12 countries** was fragmented. Matt managed a **40+** blended team and defined where WebSeries configuration ended and bespoke engineering was required. He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and tax payment modules, with Message Authentication Code verification, payment-type-specific entitlements, and sanctions screening. He also designed the centralized gateway for message transformation, protocol translation, and routing to payment rails and internal compliance and settlement systems. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,000+** clients across **180+ countries**; the gateway provided a single entry point for payments across **12 countries**, replacing fragmented regional integrations.

At **Fiserv**, the **\$8.5M** white-label card portal had missed consecutive deadlines, quality was poor, and contract cancellation was on the table. Matt took over development management, re-prioritized the backlog, reset timelines, and coordinated **45 team members** and **3 external vendors** across payment processing, fraud detection, and hosting. He managed the SOA integration layer wrapping legacy mainframe COBOL into a Java EE/Spring portal through MuleSoft, Tibco, and WebMethods. Delivery stabilized within **3 months**. The program finished **3% under budget**, met all **47 acceptance criteria**, and launched with **zero critical defects**. The portal processed **\$45M** in transactions during its first month with **99.**97%** uptime**.

At **American Express**, Virtual Payments Platform adoption lagged because clients lacked SDKs, usable documentation, and a sandbox; dependency bottlenecks also delayed testing. Matt co-created the developer portal, developed Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, introduced use case-driven documentation, and built virtualized testing environments. He used Discovery and Framing workshops, Lean Product and XP practices, and a Client Onboarding Test Drive—not just a portal redesign. API trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, onboarding time declined, and the team exceeded its delivery commitment by over **261 story points**.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s an example from **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center.

The center was designed flat from day one, with autonomy at the team level and minimal middle layers. But many practitioners came from command-and-control delivery organizations. Those habits kept returning: decisions drifted upward, teams waited for direction, and bottlenecks formed where autonomy was supposed to be. Establishing the model wasn’t enough; Matt had to enforce and revalidate it repeatedly.

Matt brought product managers, designers, and engineers together in cross-functional teams with shared ownership and decision-making authority. Rather than having leaders control outcomes, he made their role facilitating decisions and removing obstacles. He established clear, flexible guidelines so teams could make decisions within project objectives, then used continuous retrospectives and user feedback to let them adjust how they worked.

As the center scaled to **150+ practitioners**, some people still feared blame and hesitated to propose ideas or take risks. Matt spoke with team members about their challenges and aspirations, held open retrospectives focused on growth-oriented feedback, and shared his own experiences with mistakes and risk-taking. Team members were encouraged to challenge assumptions without fear of judgment.

Decentralized decision-making removed bottlenecks. Teams reported higher engagement and satisfaction and consistently met project milestones. The work to address fear of blame also improved morale, increased contributions of new ideas, and reduced turnover.

🐾 Here’s an example from **Accenture**’s Cloud Innovation Center.

Matt designed the center to be flat from day one, with team-level autonomy and collective ownership. But many practitioners arrived from command-and-control delivery organizations. Decisions started drifting upward, teams waited for direction, and bottlenecks formed where autonomy was supposed to be. As the centers scaled to **150+ practitioners**, some team members also hesitated to share ideas or take risks because they feared blame. Establishing the model wasn’t enough; putting it into practice required repeated enforcement and revalidation.

Matt put product managers, designers, and engineers together with shared decision-making authority. Anchors and team leads focused on removing obstacles rather than controlling outcomes. He made the boundaries explicit: teams could decide how to proceed while staying within project objectives.

He also regularly met with team members to understand their challenges and aspirations. In open retrospectives, people could raise concerns and suggest changes without blame. Matt shared his own experiences with mistakes and risk-taking, rather than asking others to be vulnerable while keeping his own mistakes out of view. Pair programming, collaborative coding, and iterative feedback were embedded in daily delivery.

Decentralized decision-making removed bottlenecks, and teams reported higher engagement and satisfaction. The balanced-team work reduced handoffs and project delays and achieved **zero-defect production code**. Across the center, Matt reported **4x delivery acceleration** once teams embraced lean product and modern engineering practices—not an overnight change.

🐾 Here’s how Matt built the organization.

The Cloud Innovation Center expansion started with a **10-person** pilot—not **4**—and grew to **150+** practitioners across engineering, architecture, product, and design. At **Accenture**, growing client demand required new centers in Atlanta and Tampa, but many hires lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience. Matt also needed to run hiring, development, evaluation, and promotion without adding layers of management.

He built a hiring engine across **4** channels: internal bench searches, campus recruiting, contract-to-hire, and approved job requisitions. Engineers completed hands-on TDD pairing auditions; product managers and designers worked through live client briefs. Interviewers recorded independent votes, and a failed pairing audition ended the candidacy. Matt held the closing interview and made every final hiring decision. During scaling pushes, the process produced **4–6** net-new practitioners per week, with interview participation capped at **2** slots per practitioner per week to protect delivery.

New hires progressed through tailored enablement and the “I do, we do, you do” learning model, then rotated through pairing with seasoned practitioners. Training covered pair programming, TDD, CI/CD, lean product management, and user-centered design. Skills matrices, mentors, peer-led tech talks, and learning within live client projects supported continued development.

The organization stayed deliberately flat: **3** practice leads and **8–10** client delivery leads reported to Matt. Experienced engineers served as team anchors rather than another management layer. Monday allocation reviews assigned practitioners across client work, training, and accelerator development. Because managers did not sit on daily teams, performance evaluation used evidence from recent pair partners, product managers, and anchors—not visibility to the boss. Matt ran feedback capture, promotion calibration, compensation allocation, and remediation decisions.

Over about **4 years**, the centers grew to **150+** practitioners, with near-zero attrition in the first **2 years**. Their **10-person** balanced teams delivered equivalent output to traditional **20-person** teams, with **4X** faster velocity and zero-defect deployments.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt built the organization.

For the Cloud Innovation Centers specifically, Matt grew a **10-person** pilot to **150+** practitioners across engineering, product, and design—not an engineering-only team starting at **4**. He built the Atlanta and Tampa centers at **Accenture** over about **4 years**. Growing client demand meant hiring quickly, but many new joiners lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience. Meanwhile, the deliberately flat organization had no managers sitting on daily teams, so hiring, development, and performance feedback needed mechanisms other than supervisor observation.

Matt built a hiring engine across **4** channels: internal bench search, campus recruiting, contract-to-hire, and approved job requisitions. Engineers completed hands-on TDD pairing auditions; product managers and designers worked through live scoping exercises. Interviewers recorded independent votes, and Matt conducted the closing interview and made every final hiring decision. During scaling pushes, the process added **4–6** practitioners per week. Interview duties were capped at **2** slots per practitioner weekly so recruiting did not burn out the delivery teams.

New hires received tailored enablement, then rotated through pairing with seasoned practitioners. Training covered lean product management, user-centered design, pair programming, TDD, and CI/CD. The “I do, we do, you do” model moved practitioners from guided work to independent delivery, while skills matrices and career frameworks made development expectations explicit.

Matt kept the organization flat through **3** practice leads and **8–10** client delivery leads. Experienced engineers served as team anchors rather than another management layer. Weekly allocation reviews matched people to client work, training, and internal R&D. Practice leads held career-development conversations, while performance reviews drew on evidence from recent pairing partners—not visibility to a boss.

The organization reached **150+** practitioners with near-zero attrition in its first **2 years** and multiple hires promoted. Its **10-person** balanced teams delivered output equivalent to traditional **20-person** teams, with **4X** faster velocity and zero-defect deployments.

🐾 Here’s how Matt built the organization.

The growth wasn’t a single engineering team expanding from **4** people. Matt’s earlier scope included a **3–5**-person interface team at **AT&T** and larger blended onshore/offshore delivery teams. At **Accenture’s** Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers, he grew an initial **10**-person pilot to **150+** practitioners across engineering, architecture, product, and design over about **4 years**.

Growing client demand required hiring people who often lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience, while continuing client delivery. The organization was deliberately flat: managers weren’t sitting on daily teams, so Matt needed explicit mechanisms for hiring, development, evaluation, and promotion—not additional management layers.

He built a hiring engine using bench searches, campus recruiting, contract-to-hire, and job requisitions. Engineers completed hands-on TDD pairing auditions; product managers and designers worked through live scoping exercises. Matt held the closing interview and made the final decision on every offer. During scaling pushes, the process handled **15–20 auditions per week**, producing **4–6 net-new practitioners per week**. Interview participation was capped at **2 slots per practitioner per week** to protect delivery.

Enablement combined technical training, user-centered design, lean product development, pair programming, TDD, and CI/CD. Rotating training cohorts typically ran around **8 weeks**, adjusted for skill gaps. Junior hires worked with experienced mentors through an “I do, we do, you do” learning model, progressing from guided to independent delivery.

Matt ran the organization through **11–13** direct-report practice and client leads. Experienced team anchors kept leads informed without adding middle management. Monday allocation reviews assigned practitioners across client work, training, and accelerator development. Peer feedback from recent pairing partners informed evaluations; career frameworks and calibration panels governed promotions.

The centers reached **150+ practitioners**, with near-zero attrition in the first **2 years**. Across **30+ product engagements** for **15+ Fortune **500 client**s**, **10**-person balanced teams delivered output equivalent to traditional **20**-person teams, with **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt built the teams and the organization around them.

Matt’s scope grew from small delivery teams—including a **3–5-person** interface team at **AT&T**—to **150+ practitioners** at **Accenture’s** Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers. The CIC itself grew from a **10-person** pilot, and its population included engineering, architecture, product, and design—not engineers alone.

Growing client demand required recruiting people who often lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience. Meanwhile, the deliberately flat organization had no managers sitting on daily teams. Matt needed hiring, development, evaluation, and promotion processes without adding middle-management layers.

He built a hiring engine across **4** channels: internal bench search, campus recruiting, contract-to-hire, and governed job requisitions. Engineers completed hands-on TDD pairing auditions; product managers and designers worked through live scoping exercises. Interviewers recorded independent votes, and a failed pairing audition ended the candidacy. Matt held the closing interview and made every final hiring decision. During scaling pushes, **15–20 auditions per week** produced **4–6 net-new practitioners per week**, with interview participation capped at **2 slots per practitioner per week** to protect delivery.

New joiners learned through tailored enablement, round-robin pairing with seasoned practitioners, and “I do, we do, you do.” Senior–junior coaching, peer-led tech talks, and live client projects carried learning into daily work. Balanced teams combined product, engineering, and design, using pair programming, TDD, and CI/CD.

The organization ran through **11–13 direct-report practice and client leads**. Team anchors kept leads informed without another management layer; Monday allocation reviews assigned practitioners across client work and internal R&D. Because managers did not observe daily work, Matt built evaluations around evidence from recent pair partners, product managers, and anchors, then ran feedback capture, promotion calibration, and compensation allocation.

Over about **4 years**, the CIC reached **150+ practitioners**, with near-zero attrition in the first **2 years**. Its **10-person** balanced teams delivered equivalent output to traditional **20-person** teams, with **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s Matt’s payments work at **JP Morgan Chase** and **American Express**.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, ACCESS Next Generation needed more than Bottomline Technologies’ out-of-box WebSeries platform. Regional payment systems had different formats, protocols, client configurations, and compliance records. Matt was Technology Delivery Lead, managing a **40+** blended team across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore, and working embedded with Bottomline’s team in Portsmouth.

He designed and delivered purpose-built ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules. That included NACHA file validation, embedded foreign-exchange rate visibility, Message Authentication Code payment verification, and payment-type-specific permissions—for example, allowing wire approval without FX initiation. He integrated sanctions screening and customer risk scores into payment workflows, with required approvals before high-risk or high-value payments could be released.

Rather than retain fragmented point-to-point integrations, Matt designed a centralized gateway for message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**. He also led payments-workstream data migration, preserving client configurations, entitlements, transaction histories, and compliance traceability **without disruption to live payment operations**. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, consolidating regional systems into a portal serving **135,**000+ client**s** across **180+ countries**.

At **American Express**, the Virtual Payments Platform was replacing a legacy mainframe system, but adoption lagged: clients lacked SDKs, documentation was fragmented, and there was no sandbox. Dependency bottlenecks also delayed integration testing.

Matt co-created a developer portal with Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, sample integrations, use-case-driven documentation, and a secure sandbox with refreshed client data. Environment virtualization reduced downstream dependencies so developers could test earlier. CI/CD kept documentation and APIs updated with backend changes, and a Client Onboarding Test Drive gathered end-user feedback.

API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, and client onboarding time decreased. On the portal modernization work, Lean Product and XP practices helped the team deliver over **261 additional story points** beyond its delivery commitment.

🐾 Here’s how the two engagements compare.

Both involved Execution & Delivery; **Fiserv** also involved Org & Working-Model Transformation. The starting problems differed: **Fiserv** needed recovery of a failing card-portal program, while **JP Morgan Chase** needed purpose-built payment capabilities and consolidation of fragmented regional systems into ACCESS.

At **Fiserv**, Matt took over as Development Manager after repeated missed deadlines, poor quality, and threats of contract cancellation. The **45-person** team worked with **3** external vendors while payment processing was moving from the VisionPLUS mainframe to an SOA-based API architecture. Matt reset the backlog and timelines, coordinated vendor dependencies, and managed the integration layer connecting legacy payment processing to the Java EE/Spring portal. He replaced **6-month** waterfall release cycles and a **200-page** requirements document with persona-based user stories, JIRA workflows, and **2-week** sprints within **3 months**. Early demos surfaced branding and accessibility issues; he also led semantic HTML refactoring, established accessibility guidelines, and trained teams to maintain ADA/AODA compliance across client brands from a single codebase.

The **\$8.5M** program finished **3% under budget**, met **47/47 acceptance criteria**, and launched with **zero critical defects**. The portal processed **\$45M** in its first month at **99.**97%** uptime**. A recovered release avoided **\$500K** in penalties, and the engagement secured a **\$3M** contract extension.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, Matt was Technology Delivery Lead for a **40+** blended team, spending **70–80%** of his time embedded with Bottomline Technologies. Rather than deploying WebSeries out of the box, he delivered bespoke ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and tax-payment modules, MAC security, granular entitlements, and compliance integrations. He also designed the centralized gateway for message transformation and routing across **12 countries**, and led payments-workstream migration while preserving client configurations, transaction histories, and regulatory traceability.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, consolidating regional systems into a unified portal serving **135,**000+ client**s** across **180+ countries**. Migration completed without disruption to live payments. **Fiserv’s** reported results center on recovery, cost, quality, and operating performance; ACCESS’s center on payment capabilities, global reach, and uninterrupted consolidation.

Recovering a delayed release avoided **\$500K** in penalties; the engagement secured a **\$3M** extension. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, consolidating regional systems into a unified portal serving **135,**000+ client**s** across **180+ countries**, with compliance traceability preserved through migration.

🐾 Here’s how Matt made the investment case.

The stories describe cost-versus-benefit comparisons and measured delivery economics—not a specific ROI formula, percentage return, or payback-period calculation.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Centers, clients questioned whether pair programming justified its cost. Matt addressed that concern by demonstrating velocity gains and quality improvements that offset the investment, rather than relying on presentations about methodology. He used small **4–8-week** discovery engagements to prove value before expanding into larger transformation programs, and defined a “CIC Standard of Value” with measurable delivery commitments.

The comparisons included **4X faster velocity** against traditional approaches, **10-person** balanced teams delivering equivalent output to traditional **20-person** teams, and **zero-defect deployments** through test-driven development and automated pipelines. Full MVP delivery took approximately **16–**18 week**s**. Those were delivery measures supporting the investment case—not a stated financial ROI percentage. Matt also owned the centers’ budget, cost management, chargeability, unbillable downtime, and contractor-spend approvals. The centers contributed to **\$100M+** in repeatable business through delivery excellence and client advocacy.

At **RBC**, Matt used a transparent “cost-to-fix vs. benefit comparison,” supported by code reviews, architectural heat maps, and target-state models. The assessment found that WebSeries could not meet the bank’s requirements, preventing investment in that platform path; no dollar savings were recorded.

At **Fiserv**, the financial results were explicit: an **\$8.5M** program finished **3% under budget**, preserving **\$255K** in margin, avoiding **\$500K** in contractual penalties, and securing a **\$3M** extension. Those are separate financial outcomes, not a combined ROI calculation.

The existing systems had performance and scalability limitations and lacked digital offerings. Leadership needed to know whether Bottomline WebSeries could meet the bank’s requirements before committing further investment.

Matt assessed Data, Application, Technology, and Business Architecture; reviewed code and documentation; and interviewed stakeholders. He created architectural heat maps showing gaps between requirements and platform capabilities. Working with **RBC’s** enterprise architecture team, he delivered logical and system models for a target system with the cost-to-fix versus benefit comparison. He then conducted workshops with bank leadership to connect the technical findings with business goals. The assessment found that WebSeries lacked the required modularity, and **RBC** redirected technical resources toward higher-priority initiatives rather than continuing that platform investment.

For engagement economics, Matt tracked staffing costs, forecasts against actuals, contingency, and scope changes. At **Fiserv**, the **\$8.5M** program finished **3%** under budget, preserving **\$255K** in margin and avoiding **\$500K** in contractual penalties. The recovery also secured a **\$3M** contract extension. Those are separate financial outcomes—not a stated ROI percentage, and the extension is not identified as profit.

The accounts describe the cost-benefit comparison and financial controls, but do not specify an ROI formula, benefit valuation assumptions, discount rate, or payback period.
